items.title: 6.2.2 Rule for Writing the Equation of a Tangent to a Circle

source_refs.note: Book p. 175: 6.2.2 substitution rule (i)-(v) for the tangent at (x1, y1); Note box: rule holds for all conics

blocks.text:
We have proved above that the equation of the tangent to the circle
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\]
at the point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) is:
\[xx_{1} + yy_{1} + g(x + x_{1}) + f(y + y_{1}) + c = 0\]
This can be obtained from the equation of the circle by making the following substitutions:

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The rule holds for all second-degree curves (conics) as well.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why the rule works: substitute and compare with 6.2.1(b).
\(x^{2} \to xx_{1}\) and \(y^{2} \to yy_{1}\) give \(xx_{1} + yy_{1}\).
\(2gx \to 2g \cdot \frac{x + x_{1}}{2} = g(x + x_{1})\).
\(2fy \to 2f \cdot \frac{y + y_{1}}{2} = f(y + y_{1})\).
\(c\) stays \(c\). Put together, this is exactly the tangent we derived. So the rule is not a new fact, only a quick way to remember the formula.
Each square is shared out as "one copy of the variable, one copy of the point", and each single \(x\) or \(y\) is replaced by the average of the variable and the point's coordinate.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration (not from the book): tangent to \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 4x - 6y - 12 = 0\) at \((1, -1)\).
Check the point: \(1 + 1 + 4 + 6 - 12 = 0\), so it is on the circle.
Apply the rule (\(x_{1} = 1\), \(y_{1} = -1\)):
\[x(1) + y(-1) + 4\cdot\dfrac{x + 1}{2} - 6\cdot\dfrac{y - 1}{2} - 12 = 0\]
\[x - y + 2x + 2 - 3y + 3 - 12 = 0\]
\[3x - 4y - 7 = 0\]
Check: the centre is \((-2, 3)\); the radius to \((1, -1)\) has slope \(\frac{-1 - 3}{1 + 2} = -\frac{4}{3}\) and the tangent has slope \(\frac{3}{4}\); the product is \(-1\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text:
If the circle is written as \(Ax^{2} + Ay^{2} + Dx + Ey + F = 0\) with \(A \ne 1\), you may divide by \(A\) first, or apply the substitutions directly (\(Ax^{2} \to Axx_{1}\), and so on); both give the same line.
For the other conics of this unit the same rule applies, and a product term \(xy\), if present, is replaced by \(\frac{xy_{1} + x_{1}y}{2}\) (our addition).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Tangent at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) on a circle: in the circle's equation replace \(x^{2}\) by \(xx_{1}\), \(y^{2}\) by \(yy_{1}\), \(x\) by \(\frac{x + x_{1}}{2}\), \(y\) by \(\frac{y + y_{1}}{2}\); keep \(c\).
2. The rule reproduces the formula of 6.2.1 exactly.
3. It works only at a point on the curve.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Replacing \(x\) by \(x + x_{1}\) (forgetting to halve). Then \(2gx\) wrongly becomes \(2g(x + x_{1})\).
2. Also changing the constant term. The constant \(c\) stays exactly as it is.
3. Using the rule for a point outside the circle: the line obtained is then not a tangent (it is the chord of contact, see Example 12).
